passage: "Preeti, you know what my mother says every time I mention investing? 'Buy gold. Put it in a fixed deposit. Done.' I used to roll my eyes. I'm Sarika, I work in marketing, I watch finance videos, I thought she was stuck in 1995. Then last Diwali she told me something she'd never said before. When I was small, my father put all their savings into a chit fund a neighbour ran. It vanished. They had to sell her wedding bangles to pay school fees. That's why gold feels safe to her. I felt ashamed of my eye-rolling. So I didn't dismiss her anymore. But I didn't blindly follow her either. I went with her to a registered adviser at our bank. We learned about a few options together. I'm starting small and slow, and keeping some in the things she trusts too. She actually asked questions. That felt good."

I'm Simran, and last year I lost most of my savings on a tip from a trading group. A stranger posted charts, people cheered, and I put in two years of savings in one afternoon. Two weeks later it was worth almost nothing.
Looking back, the loss wasn't the worst part. The hiding was. I told my flatmate Urmila I was "just tired". I kept checking the app at night, thinking about putting in more to win it back.
Then one night Urmila found me crying in the kitchen and made me talk. She didn't lecture. She said, "My uncle did the same. It happens to lots of people." That helped.
We wrote down what happened: who gave the tip, what I didn't check, why I rushed. I left the trading group. I met a registered adviser. Now I save a fixed amount each month, and I don't invest in anything I can't explain to Urmila in two sentences.

qa.q: How much did Simran put in that afternoon?
qa.a: Two years of savings, in one afternoon.

qa.a: Simran felt ashamed and trapped, pretending to be tired and tempted to put in more to win it back.

Sarika's diary, 3 a.m.
Sharmila found my trading app open tonight. The screen showed everything: the options, the losses from last month I hadn't mentioned.
She didn't shout. She just said, very quietly, "How long have you been doing this without telling me?" And her hands were shaking.
My first instinct was to say, "It's my money, it's under control." I actually started saying it. Then I saw her face. She wasn't accusing me. She was frightened.
So I shut up and listened. She talked about her father, who lost their house to bad bets. I never knew the full story.
We made a plan before bed:
- I show her everything I hold, tomorrow.
- We agree together on a small amount I can play with, and I stop at that.
- We see a proper adviser together next week.
I feel embarrassed. But also lighter. Hiding it was the heavy part.

I'm Madhav, and the call came from Gopika-mami at 9 p.m. She was crying. A man had said her grandson was in a police station and needed bail money sent right away. She had already sent twenty thousand and was about to send more.
My first thought, honestly, was: Mami, how could you? We've warned you. I bit it back.
"Mami, don't send anything else. I'm coming."
When I got there, she was sitting by the phone, ashamed. "I'm a foolish old woman."
"No. They're professionals. They fool clever people every day."
We called her bank to block further payments and dispute the transfer, then filed a report on the cybercrime helpline. Then I called her grandson, who was fine, at college.
Before I left, we wrote a card for her phone table: "Anyone asks for money urgently? Hang up. Call Madhav." She laughed, a little. Looking back, the card mattered more than my warnings ever had.

Supervisor's note, Thursday, 4 p.m.
Chinmay, junior analyst, came back from lunch pale and couldn't focus. When I asked, he said he'd paid a "customs fee" to someone claiming his parcel was held, and then paid again when they said it was "flagged". He kept saying, "I'm so stupid."
His teammate Mridul was already beside him. I watched Mridul pull up a chair and say, "No, you're not. These people are good at this." Mridul didn't mention that he had warned the team about this very scam last month.
Mridul helped Chinmay call the bank's official helpline to block his card and dispute the payment, then helped him file a complaint on the cybercrime portal. Afterwards, he showed Chinmay how to check a courier's real tracking site before paying anything.
I gave Chinmay the rest of the afternoon off. Mridul will present a short safety talk to the team on Monday.

qa.a: He reassured him without blame, helped him block the card and dispute the payment, filed a cybercrime complaint with him, and showed him how to check a courier's real site.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel after Mridul's help?
qa.a: Chinmay probably feels relieved and less alone, with a bit more confidence about spotting scams next time.
